topic: S3.1 The periodic table: Classification of elements
subject: chemistry

items.q: Which element is classified as a metalloid?
items.correct: Silicon
items.misconception: Aluminium
items.why: The metalloids are introduced as 'the elements along the staircase', and several metals (aluminium, and at the bottom polonium) also border the line, so students classify by adjacency rather than by properties. The stepped line is a boundary drawn between metals and non-metals; the metalloids are the specific elements with intermediate properties that lie along it. Aluminium borders the line on the metal side and has typical metallic properties.
items.specStatementText: The periodic table consists of periods, groups and blocks.
items.random_wrong: Iodine

items.q: Gallium (Z = 31) has the electron configuration [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p¹. Which statement classifies gallium correctly?
items.correct: A p-block metal, as its last electron enters the 4p sublevel
items.misconception: A p-block non-metal, as metals are in the s- and d-blocks
items.why: The most familiar p-block elements (oxygen, nitrogen, the halogens and noble gases) are non-metals, and simplified diagrams colour the whole right-hand block as 'non-metals'. Metallic character increases down each p-block group. The stepped line crosses the p-block, so its lower-left elements, including aluminium and gallium, are metals.
items.specStatementText: The periodic table consists of periods, groups and blocks.
items.random_wrong: A p-block metalloid, as it borders the stepped metal/non-metal line

items.q: Selenium is in period 4 and group 16 of the periodic table. Which statement about a selenium atom is correct?
items.correct: It has six valence electrons, in the fourth energy level
items.misconception: It has sixteen valence electrons, in the fourth energy level
items.why: Earlier courses number the main groups I to VIII (or 1 to 8), where the number does equal the valence electrons. Carried over to the 1–18 numbering the rule fails, but students keep applying it. With groups numbered 1 to 18, the ten d-block columns (groups 3–12) sit between groups 2 and 13. So a p-block atom has (group number − 10) valence electrons: group 16, six; group 17, seven. Group 7 (manganese) is in the d-block, not the halogens.
items.specStatementText: The period number shows the outer energy level that is occupied by electrons. Elements in a group have a common number of valence electrons.
items.random_wrong: It has four valence electrons, located in the sixth energy level

items.q: Which element is a halogen?
items.correct: Iodine
items.misconception: Krypton
items.why: The two groups are adjacent at the right of the table, both contain gases at room temperature, and both are met together when discussing full or nearly full outer shells. Group 17 atoms have seven valence electrons and are reactive, forming X⁻ ions and X₂ molecules; group 18 atoms have a full outer level and are very unreactive. The names apply to different groups.
items.specStatementText: The period number shows the outer energy level that is occupied by electrons. Elements in a group have a common number of valence electrons.
items.random_wrong: Manganese

items.q: How, and why, does atomic radius change across period 3 from sodium to chlorine?
items.correct: It decreases, as nuclear charge rises while electrons enter the same level
items.misconception: It increases, as each atom has more electrons, which need more space
items.why: Everyday experience says that adding more material makes an object bigger, and down a group atoms do get bigger as electrons are added, so students generalize this to periods. Size depends on how strongly the outer electrons are attracted, not on how many there are. Across a period, electrons enter the same level while the nuclear charge rises, so radius decreases; down a group, a new energy level is occupied, so radius increases.
items.specStatementText: Periodicity refers to trends in properties of elements across a period and down a group.
items.random_wrong: It increases, as the nucleus's attraction is shared out among more electrons

items.q: The ions Na⁺, F⁻, Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ all have the electron configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶. Which lists them in order of decreasing ionic radius?
items.correct: O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺
items.misconception: O²⁻ = F⁻ = Na⁺ = Mg²⁺
items.why: Students learn that the electron arrangement determines chemical behaviour and assume it also determines size, forgetting that the nucleus pulls on those electrons. Radius depends on how strongly the nucleus attracts the electrons. In the series O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺ the configuration is the same but nuclear charge increases, so radius decreases.
items.specStatementText: Periodicity refers to trends in properties of elements across a period and down a group.
items.random_wrong: Mg²⁺ > Na⁺ > F⁻ > O²⁻

items.q: Which element has the highest electronegativity on the Pauling scale?
items.correct: Fluorine, F
items.misconception: Neon, Ne
items.why: Students extend a learned trend to every element in the period without checking whether the property applies to it. Electronegativity is defined for atoms in covalent bonds. The trend increases across a period up to group 17; the noble gases (helium, neon, argon) are not assigned Pauling values.
items.specStatementText: Periodicity refers to trends in properties of elements across a period and down a group.
items.random_wrong: Chlorine, Cl

items.q: How does the first ionization energy of rubidium (Z = 37) compare with that of sodium (Z = 11)?
items.correct: Lower, as rubidium's outer electron is further out and more shielded
items.misconception: Higher, as rubidium's nucleus carries a much larger positive charge
items.why: Students correctly learn that nuclear charge increases attraction across a period and apply it on its own down a group, overlooking distance and shielding. Consider all three factors. Across a period only the nuclear charge changes significantly. Down a group the increase in distance and shielding dominates, so ionization energy and electronegativity decrease.
items.specStatementText: Periodicity refers to trends in properties of elements across a period and down a group.
items.random_wrong: Equal, as each atom loses one electron to gain a noble-gas configuration

items.q: A small piece of sodium is added to a large volume of water containing universal indicator. Which statement describes what happens?
items.correct: Hydrogen and sodium hydroxide form, so the solution turns alkaline
items.misconception: Hydrogen and sodium oxide form, and the oxide stays as a solid
items.why: Students know that water contains oxygen and that metals form oxides when they burn, and they know that heated magnesium with steam gives magnesium oxide, so they transfer that product to group 1 metals in cold water. Group 1 metals react with cold water to form the hydroxide and hydrogen. Even the oxide itself would react with water to form the hydroxide: Na₂O(s) + H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq).
items.specStatementText: Trends in properties of elements down a group include the increasing metallic character of group 1 elements and decreasing non-metallic character of group 17 elements.
items.random_wrong: Hydrogen gas is released, so the solution turns acidic

items.q: Bromine water is added separately to aqueous potassium chloride and to aqueous potassium iodide. Which observation is expected?
items.correct: A reaction occurs with the potassium iodide only
items.misconception: A reaction occurs with the potassium chloride only
items.why: Group 1 is usually taught first and its dramatic trend (lithium to potassium) is memorable, so students generalize 'more reactive further down' to all groups. Ask whether the element reacts by losing or by gaining electrons. Down any group the outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded: electrons are lost more easily (metals more reactive) but gained less readily (non-metals less reactive).
items.specStatementText: Trends in properties of elements down a group include the increasing metallic character of group 1 elements and decreasing non-metallic character of group 17 elements.
items.random_wrong: There is no reaction with either of the two solutions

items.q: Sulfur dioxide released by burning fossil fuels contributes to acid rain. What is formed when sulfur dioxide itself reacts with water, before any oxidation takes place?
items.correct: Sulfurous acid, which makes the solution acidic
items.misconception: Sulfuric acid, which makes the solution acidic
items.why: Sulfuric acid is the familiar laboratory acid and is often named as the main acid in acid rain, while the names 'sulfurous' and 'sulfuric' differ by only a few letters. Match the oxidation state: sulfur is +4 in SO₂ and in H₂SO₃ (sulfurous acid), and +6 in SO₃ and in H₂SO₄ (sulfuric acid). In the atmosphere, SO₂ is partly oxidized to SO₃ before forming sulfuric acid.
items.specStatementText: Metallic and non-metallic properties show a continuum. This includes the trend from basic metal oxides through amphoteric to acidic non-metal oxides.
items.random_wrong: Sulfur hydroxide, which makes the solution alkaline

items.q: Which statement about ocean acidification is correct?
items.correct: Dissolved CO₂ forms carbonic acid, lowering the pH, but seawater stays alkaline
items.misconception: Seawater has now become acidic, with a pH below 7, because of absorbed CO₂
items.why: In everyday language '-ification' suggests turning into something, so 'acidification' is read as 'becoming an acid', and the small pH numbers involved are rarely quoted. Acidification describes the direction of change: the concentration of H⁺ ions increases and the pH decreases. Seawater has become less alkaline, which still harms organisms that build calcium carbonate shells.
items.specStatementText: Metallic and non-metallic properties show a continuum. This includes the trend from basic metal oxides through amphoteric to acidic non-metal oxides.
items.random_wrong: Acid rain falling on the sea is the main cause of the fall in seawater pH

items.q: What is the oxidation state of nitrogen in the nitrite ion?
items.why:
The first rule practised is 'oxidation states in a compound sum to zero', and students apply it to ions without adjusting for the charge. Use 'sum = overall charge': zero for a neutral compound, the ion's charge for an ion. For SO₃²⁻, x + 3(−2) = −2, so sulfur is +4.

Working: The nitrite ion is NO₂⁻. Oxygen is −2 and the oxidation states sum to the charge on the ion: x + 2(−2) = −1, so x = +3.
items.specStatementText: The oxidation state is a number assigned to an atom to show the number of electrons transferred in forming a bond. It is the charge that atom would have if the compound were composed of ions.
items.working: The nitrite ion is NO₂⁻. Oxygen is −2 and the oxidation states sum to the charge on the ion: x + 2(−2) = −1, so x = +3.

items.q: What are the oxidation states of hydrogen in sodium hydride, NaH, and of oxygen in sodium peroxide, Na₂O₂?
items.why:
Hydrogen is met almost entirely in acids and in compounds with non-metals (water, ammonia, methane), where it is +1, and it sits in group 1 above the metals that form 1+ ions. Hydrogen takes −1 when bonded to a metal less electronegative than itself. In NaH, sodium is +1, so hydrogen must be −1 for the compound to be neutral.

Working: NaH: Na is +1 and the compound is neutral, so H = 0 − (+1) = −1. Na₂O₂: 2(+1) + 2x = 0, so x = −1.
items.specStatementText: The oxidation state is a number assigned to an atom to show the number of electrons transferred in forming a bond. It is the charge that atom would have if the compound were composed of ions.
items.working: NaH: Na is +1 and the compound is neutral, so H = 0 − (+1) = −1. Na₂O₂: 2(+1) + 2x = 0, so x = −1.

items.q: Every atom in an uncombined element, such as O₂ or Cl₂, has an oxidation state of zero. Why?
items.correct: Its atoms are all identical, so no electrons are transferred between them
items.misconception: It has no overall charge, so each of its atoms must also be zero
items.why: Students confuse the oxidation state of an atom with the overall charge of the species, because both are described as 'charges'. Oxidation states are assigned atom by atom; only their sum must equal the overall charge. Water is neutral, yet hydrogen is +1 and oxygen −2. An element is zero because bonds between identical atoms involve no transfer of electrons.
items.specStatementText: The oxidation state is a number assigned to an atom to show the number of electrons transferred in forming a bond. It is the charge that atom would have if the compound were composed of ions.
items.random_wrong: Oxidation states are given only to ions, and it contains none

items.q: The first ionization energies of magnesium and aluminium are 738 kJ mol⁻¹ and 578 kJ mol⁻¹. Which explanation of the lower value for aluminium is correct?
items.correct: Aluminium's electron is removed from 3p, higher in energy than magnesium's 3s
items.misconception: Magnesium's filled 3s sublevel has a special stability that resists ionization
items.why: The phrase 'half-filled and filled sublevels are especially stable' is widespread in textbooks and websites, and it seems to account neatly for the anomalies in chromium and copper as well. Explain each discontinuity by comparing the energies of the electrons removed. Mg → Al: the 3p electron of aluminium is higher in energy than the 3s electron of magnesium. P → S: the paired 3p electron of sulfur is raised in energy by electron–electron repulsion.
items.specStatementText: Discontinuities occur in the trend of increasing first ionization energy across a period.
items.random_wrong: Aluminium's electron is removed from a paired orbital, where repulsion aids removal

items.q: The first ionization energies of phosphorus and sulfur are 1012 kJ mol⁻¹ and 1000 kJ mol⁻¹. Which explanation of the lower value for sulfur is correct?
items.correct: Sulfur loses an electron from a doubly occupied 3p orbital, where repulsion raises its energy
items.misconception: Sulfur's electron is removed from a sublevel of higher energy than phosphorus's
items.why: The two discontinuities are learned together, and students memorize two explanations without linking each to the orbital occupancy of the atoms concerned. Write the outer configurations: Mg 3s², Al 3s² 3p¹ (new sublevel, single electron); P 3s² 3p³ (three unpaired 3p electrons), S 3s² 3p⁴ (one 3p orbital now paired). The configuration shows which explanation applies.
items.specStatementText: Discontinuities occur in the trend of increasing first ionization energy across a period.
items.random_wrong: Phosphorus's half-filled 3p sublevel has a special stability that resists ionization

items.q: Which statement describes a characteristic property of the transition elements?
items.correct: Many of them and their compounds act as catalysts
items.misconception: Their catalysts are consumed, so they must be added in excess
items.why: Students learn that catalysts 'take part' in reactions, and anything that takes part in a reaction seems to be consumed; catalysts are also replaced in industry, suggesting they run out. A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy and is recovered chemically unchanged at the end. Industrial catalysts are replaced because they become poisoned or worn, not because the reaction consumes them.
items.specStatementText: Transition elements have incomplete d-sublevels that give them characteristic properties.
items.random_wrong: All of their compounds are coloured, even those of Sc³⁺

items.q: Iron has the electron configuration [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². Which statement about the formation of the Fe³⁺ ion is correct?
items.correct: Both 4s electrons and then one 3d electron are removed, giving [Ar] 3d⁵
items.misconception: Three electrons are removed from the 3d sublevel, giving [Ar] 3d³ 4s²
items.why: The aufbau order (4s before 3d) is learned as a filling sequence, and 'last in, first out' is an intuitive rule for undoing it; the 4s/3d ordering is widely discussed as a source of confusion in chemistry teaching. Once electrons occupy the 3d sublevel, the 4s electrons are the higher in energy and are further from the nucleus on average, so they are removed first. Write the atom's configuration, then remove 4s electrons before any 3d electrons.
items.specStatementText: The formation of variable oxidation states in transition elements can be explained by the fact that their successive ionization energies are close in value.
items.random_wrong: Three electrons are added to the 3d sublevel, giving [Ar] 3d⁹ 4s²

items.q: Manganese forms compounds in oxidation states from +2 to +7. Which statement explains why transition elements show variable oxidation states?
items.correct: Their 4s and 3d electrons are close in energy, so successive ionization energies are close in value
items.misconception: They lose different numbers of electrons, each ion reaching a stable noble-gas configuration
items.why: The octet rule is taught early as a way of predicting formulae, and the language of atoms 'wanting' or 'needing' electrons turns it into a cause. This is widely reported in chemistry-education research as an 'octet framework'. The octet rule predicts many formulae but does not explain them. Explain with forces: a greater nuclear charge at the same distance and shielding holds electrons more strongly; a larger distance or more shielding holds them less strongly. Energy changes, not a desire for full shells, decide whether a process happens.
items.specStatementText: The formation of variable oxidation states in transition elements can be explained by the fact that their successive ionization energies are close in value.
items.random_wrong: Their 3d electrons, filled last, are the outermost and are removed first in any number

items.q: A solution of a transition element complex looks blue in white light. On the colour wheel, blue is opposite orange. Which statement explains the blue colour?
items.correct: It absorbs orange light as electrons are promoted between split d orbitals
items.misconception: It absorbs blue light as electrons are promoted between split d orbitals
items.why: Students think of a coloured substance as 'having' or 'taking in' its colour, and the word 'absorbs' is attached to the colour they can see. Use the colour wheel: the colour observed is opposite (complementary to) the colour absorbed. A red solution absorbs green; a blue solution absorbs orange; a violet solution absorbs yellow.
items.specStatementText: Transition element complexes are coloured due to the absorption of light when an electron is promoted between the orbitals in the split d-sublevels. The colour absorbed is complementary to the colour observed.
items.random_wrong: Its electrons fall back between split d orbitals, emitting blue light

items.q: A solution of a transition element complex appears red. On the colour wheel, red is opposite green. Take the wavelength of green light as 530 nm and of red light as 700 nm, and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. What is the frequency of the light absorbed most strongly?
items.why:
Nano- and micro- are both prefixes for very small quantities and are met far less often than milli- and kilo-, so their powers of ten are easily confused; power-of-ten slips in unit conversions are a common source of lost marks in calculations. Learn the prefixes as a ladder: milli 10⁻³, micro 10⁻⁶, nano 10⁻⁹, pico 10⁻¹². So 530 nm = 530 × 10⁻⁹ m = 5.30 × 10⁻⁷ m.

Working: The colour absorbed is complementary to the colour observed: red is seen, so green light is absorbed, λ = 530 nm = 530 × 10⁻⁹ m = 5.30 × 10⁻⁷ m. f = c/λ = (3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)/(5.30 × 10⁻⁷ m) = 5.66 × 10¹⁴ s⁻¹ = 5.66 × 10¹⁴ Hz.
items.specStatementText: Transition element complexes are coloured due to the absorption of light when an electron is promoted between the orbitals in the split d-sublevels. The colour absorbed is complementary to the colour observed.
items.working: The colour absorbed is complementary to the colour observed: red is seen, so green light is absorbed, λ = 530 nm = 530 × 10⁻⁹ m = 5.30 × 10⁻⁷ m. f = c/λ = (3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)/(5.30 × 10⁻⁷ m) = 5.66 × 10¹⁴ s⁻¹ = 5.66 × 10¹⁴ Hz.

items.q: The first electron affinity of chlorine is −349 kJ mol⁻¹. How does the first electron affinity of bromine compare with this value, and why?
items.correct: Less negative, as the added electron enters a more distant, more shielded level
items.misconception: Less negative, as bromine's nuclear attraction is shared out among more electrons
items.why: Students picture the nuclear force as a fixed supply to be shared out. This 'conservation of force' idea is widely reported in chemistry-education research on ionization energy. Coulomb attraction between the nucleus and one electron depends on the charges and their separation. Adding electrons does not dilute it; what reduces the attraction on an outer electron is greater distance and repulsion (shielding) by inner electrons.
items.specStatementText: Periodicity refers to trends in properties of elements across a period and down a group.
items.random_wrong: More negative, as bromine's nucleus carries a larger positive charge

items.q: Small pieces of lithium and of potassium are added separately to cold water. How does the reaction of potassium compare with that of lithium, and why?
items.correct: More vigorous, as its outer electron is further out and more shielded
items.misconception: Equally vigorous, as both are group 1 metals with one outer electron
items.why: Students learn that elements in a group are similar because they have the same number of valence electrons, and 'similar' becomes 'identical'. Same number of valence electrons gives similar reactions, but the size of the atoms changes down a group and so do the properties. Down group 1 the outer electron is lost more easily, so reactivity increases; down group 17 the atoms attract an incoming electron less strongly, so oxidizing ability decreases.
items.specStatementText: Trends in properties of elements down a group include the increasing metallic character of group 1 elements and decreasing non-metallic character of group 17 elements.
items.random_wrong: Less vigorous, as its larger nuclear charge holds its outer electron more tightly

items.q: Which statement about aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃, is correct?
items.correct: It reacts with both acids and bases, since it is amphoteric
items.misconception: It reacts with acids only, as every metal oxide is basic
items.why: Earlier courses teach the binary rule 'metal oxides are basic, non-metal oxides are acidic', which works for the familiar examples (sodium, calcium and copper oxides; carbon and sulfur dioxides) and leaves no place for amphoteric oxides. Treat oxide character as a continuum: across period 3, Na₂O and MgO are basic, Al₂O₃ is amphoteric, and the oxides of phosphorus, sulfur and chlorine are acidic.
items.specStatementText: Metallic and non-metallic properties show a continuum. This includes the trend from basic metal oxides through amphoteric to acidic non-metal oxides.
items.random_wrong: It reacts with bases only, as it is a p-block non-metal oxide

items.q: Calcium oxide is added to water containing universal indicator. Which statement describes what happens?
items.correct: Calcium hydroxide forms, so the solution turns alkaline
items.misconception: The mixture fizzes, as hydrogen gas is released from the water
items.why:
The first reactions with water that students learn are those of group 1 and group 2 metals, which always give 'hydroxide + hydrogen', so this product pair is learned as the pattern for anything containing the metal. Hydrogen gas forms when something reduces the water, as a group 1 or group 2 metal does. In a metal oxide the metal is already oxidized and the oxide ion cannot reduce water, so the oxide ion simply takes H⁺ from water: O²⁻ + H₂O → 2OH⁻, and all the hydrogen ends up in the hydroxide.

Working: CaO(s) + H₂O(l) → Ca(OH)₂(aq); in solution Ca(OH)₂(aq) → Ca²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq), so the solution is alkaline. The equation balances with no H₂ as a product: 2 H atoms on each side.
items.specStatementText: Metallic and non-metallic properties show a continuum. This includes the trend from basic metal oxides through amphoteric to acidic non-metal oxides.
items.random_wrong: The oxide dissolves without reacting, so the solution stays neutral
items.working: CaO(s) + H₂O(l) → Ca(OH)₂(aq); in solution Ca(OH)₂(aq) → Ca²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq), so the solution is alkaline. The equation balances with no H₂ as a product: 2 H atoms on each side.

items.q: Copper, [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹, is a d-block element. Is copper a transition element?
items.correct: Yes, as its ion Cu²⁺, [Ar] 3d⁹, has an incomplete 3d sublevel
items.misconception: No, as its atom, [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹, has a full 3d sublevel
items.why: Electron configurations are practised mainly for atoms, and copper's atom, [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹, is memorized as an exception with a full 3d sublevel; students then test 'incomplete d sublevel' on the atom only and forget the ions. Check the atom and its common ions. Copper(II), [Ar] 3d⁹, has an incomplete 3d sublevel, so copper is a transition element; zinc's only ion, Zn²⁺, is [Ar] 3d¹⁰, so zinc is not.
items.specStatementText: Transition elements have incomplete d-sublevels that give them characteristic properties.
items.random_wrong: Yes, as every metal in the d-block is a transition element

items.q: An atom has the electron configuration [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p³. Which statement gives the group of the element correctly?
items.correct: Group 15, as its 4p³ electrons place it in the third p-block column
items.misconception: Group 12, as its full 3d sublevel places it in the d-block
items.why: Students read the block from the 'most advanced' sublevel type they can see in the configuration, and in period 4 the 3d¹⁰ stands out in the middle of the notation. Find the sublevel that the last electrons (in filling order) enter. After zinc, the 3d sublevel is full and electrons enter 4p, so gallium to krypton are p-block elements.
items.specStatementText: The period number shows the outer energy level that is occupied by electrons. Elements in a group have a common number of valence electrons.
items.random_wrong: Group 5, as its outer level holds five valence electrons

items.q: The graph shows the first ionization energies of the elements with atomic numbers 3 to 18. Which statement explains why the value at the point labelled X is lower than that of the element before it?
items.correct: Its electron is removed from a p orbital that already holds another electron, whose repulsion raises its energy
items.misconception: The element before X has a half-filled p sublevel, whose special stability makes its electron harder to remove
items.why: The phrase 'half-filled and filled sublevels are especially stable' is widespread in textbooks and websites, and it seems to account neatly for the anomalies in chromium and copper as well. Explain each discontinuity by comparing the energies of the electrons removed. Mg → Al: the 3p electron of aluminium is higher in energy than the 3s electron of magnesium. P → S: the paired 3p electron of sulfur is raised in energy by electron–electron repulsion.
items.specStatementText: Discontinuities occur in the trend of increasing first ionization energy across a period.
items.random_wrong: Its electron is removed from the p sublevel, which is higher in energy than the s sublevel of the element before X

items.q: A student shakes a small sample of each of six period 3 oxides with water and measures the pH of the mixture. The bar chart shows the readings. Two of the oxides give the same reading. Which statement about those two oxides is correct?
items.correct: Both are insoluble in water, which hides that one is amphoteric and the other acidic
items.misconception: Both are amphoteric, as their elements lie on the boundary between metals and non-metals
items.why: The continuum basic → amphoteric → acidic is taught alongside the continuum metal → metalloid → non-metal, and the two sequences are lined up, so the metalloid's oxide is placed in the middle category. Silicon dioxide's failure to change the pH of water seems to confirm that it is 'in between'. Classify an oxide by its reactions with acids and with bases, not by the element's position alone. Al₂O₃ reacts with both, so it is amphoteric; SiO₂ reacts only with bases, so it is acidic, even though it is insoluble in water. Metallic character and oxide character both change gradually, but the amphoteric point in period 3 falls at aluminium, not silicon.
items.specStatementText: Metallic and non-metallic properties show a continuum. This includes the trend from basic metal oxides through amphoteric to acidic non-metal oxides.
items.random_wrong: Both are neutral oxides, which react with neither acids nor bases and so leave water at pH 7

items.q: The diagram shows a blank outline of periods 1 to 4 of the periodic table, with the s-, d- and p-blocks labelled and four cells lettered. Which cell is occupied by an element whose atoms have six valence electrons in the third energy level?
items.correct: The cell labelled Y
items.misconception: The cell labelled W
items.why: The similar words 'valence' and 'valency' are used loosely in textbooks and class, so the count of outer electrons and the combining power are merged. Count the electrons in the outer energy level to get the valence electrons. The valency (combining power) is a separate idea; for group 16 it is 2 = 8 − 6.
items.specStatementText: The period number shows the outer energy level that is occupied by electrons. Elements in a group have a common number of valence electrons.
items.random_wrong: The cell labelled X

items.q: Iodine is a shiny, grey-black solid. Does that make it a metal or metalloid?
items.correct: No. Iodine is a non-metal: it is a molecular solid of I₂ molecules that does not conduct electricity and forms an acidic oxide. Its lustre alone does not make it metallic.
items.misconception: An element can be classified as a metal or metalloid from one visible property, such as a shiny surface.
items.why: At school, metals are first recognized by their appearance, so shininess becomes a shortcut. Iodine crystals and graphite look metallic, which reinforces the shortcut. Classification rests on the pattern of properties and on position in the periodic table: electrical conductivity, the acid–base character of the oxide and the tendency to form positive or negative ions. Iodine is in group 17, well to the non-metal side of the stepped line.
items.specStatementText: The periodic table consists of periods, groups and blocks.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are the transition elements metalloids, lying 'between' metals and non-metals?
items.correct: No. The transition elements are all metals. The metalloids lie along the stepped line in the p-block, not in the d-block.
items.misconception: Transition elements are intermediate between metals and non-metals, because 'transition' means changing from one kind to the other.
items.why: In everyday language a transition is a change from one state to another, and the d-block sits in the middle of the table between the reactive metals and the p-block, so the name seems to describe a metal-to-non-metal change. The name refers historically to the block sitting between the s- and p-blocks, not to a change in metallic character. Every d-block element is a metal; the metal-to-non-metal change occurs across the p-block, where the metalloids are found.
items.specStatementText: The periodic table consists of periods, groups and blocks.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the period number give the number of valence electrons and the group number give the outer energy level?
items.correct: No. It is the other way round: the period number is the outer energy level occupied, and the group identifies the number of valence electrons.
items.misconception: Periods and groups are interchangeable, so the period number can give the valence electrons and the group the energy level.
items.why: Both are numbers read off the table, and the words 'period' and 'group' do not themselves suggest rows or columns, so students confuse which one gives which information. Periods are rows: moving down a row adds an energy level, so the period number is the outer level. Groups are columns: elements in a column share the same number of valence electrons.
items.specStatementText: The period number shows the outer energy level that is occupied by electrons. Elements in a group have a common number of valence electrons.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is an ion or atom larger because its nucleus contains more protons and neutrons?
items.correct: No. The nucleus is tiny compared with the atom; size is set by the electron cloud. More protons for the same electrons pull the electrons in, making the particle smaller.
items.misconception: A heavier nucleus with more protons and neutrons takes up more space, so the atom or ion is larger.
items.why: Students link size with mass from everyday objects and from diagrams that draw the nucleus as a large ball, and they know that larger atoms down a group are heavier. The nucleus occupies a very small fraction of the volume of an atom. Radius is governed by the electrons and how strongly they are attracted: for the same number of electrons, a larger nuclear charge gives a smaller radius.
items.specStatementText: Periodicity refers to trends in properties of elements across a period and down a group.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are electronegativity and electron affinity the same property?
items.correct: No. Electronegativity is the ability of a bonded atom to attract a shared pair of electrons (Pauling scale, no units). Electron affinity is the energy change when gaseous atoms gain electrons (kJ mol⁻¹). Chlorine has the most negative electron affinity (−349 kJ mol⁻¹), but fluorine is the most electronegative element.
items.misconception: Electronegativity is the same as electron affinity, so the element with the most negative electron affinity is the most electronegative.
items.why: Both describe an atom's attraction for electrons and both have 'electron' in the name, and students meet the two terms together in the same lesson. Keep the definitions apart: electronegativity refers to a bonding pair in a covalent bond; electron affinity refers to an isolated gaseous atom gaining an electron. They follow similar general trends, but their values are not interchangeable, and fluorine (not chlorine) has the highest electronegativity.
items.specStatementText: Periodicity refers to trends in properties of elements across a period and down a group.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Because hydrogen gas is produced when sodium reacts with water, is the solution acidic?
items.correct: No. The solution is alkaline, because it contains hydroxide ions from the sodium hydroxide formed. Hydrogen gas is not an acid and does not make a solution acidic.
items.misconception: If a reaction produces hydrogen, the solution becomes acidic, because hydrogen is associated with acids.
items.why: Acids are defined early as substances containing or releasing hydrogen ions, and the test for hydrogen is met with acid–metal reactions, so hydrogen gas and acidity become linked. Acidity comes from H⁺(aq) ions, not from H₂ gas. In the reaction of a group 1 metal with water, hydrogen atoms from water leave as H₂ and OH⁻ ions remain, so the solution becomes alkaline.
items.specStatementText: Trends in properties of elements down a group include the increasing metallic character of group 1 elements and decreasing non-metallic character of group 17 elements.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When sodium disappears in water, is it simply dissolving?
items.correct: No. Sodium reacts chemically with water: new substances, hydrogen gas and sodium hydroxide, are formed, and the metal cannot be recovered by evaporating the water.
items.misconception: A metal that disappears in water has dissolved, like salt, and any bubbles are air or vapour escaping.
items.why: The metal disappearing into a colourless solution looks like dissolving, and the distinction between dissolving and reacting is widely reported in chemistry-education research as difficult for students. Evidence of a chemical reaction includes a gas that pops with a lighted splint (hydrogen), a change in indicator colour (hydroxide ions) and heat released. Evaporating the solution gives sodium hydroxide, not sodium.
items.specStatementText: Trends in properties of elements down a group include the increasing metallic character of group 1 elements and decreasing non-metallic character of group 17 elements.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does every oxide react with water to form a hydroxide that makes the solution alkaline?
items.correct: No. Metal oxides form hydroxides and alkaline solutions, but non-metal oxides such as CO₂ and SO₂ react with water to form acids.
items.misconception: All oxides behave like metal oxides: they react with water to form hydroxides, which are bases.
items.why: Bases are introduced as 'metal oxides and hydroxides', and the pattern oxide + water → hydroxide is practised with calcium and sodium oxides, so it is applied to every oxide. Oxide character runs from basic (metals) through amphoteric to acidic (non-metals). A non-metal oxide reacts with water to form an oxoacid, for example SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃.
items.specStatementText: Metallic and non-metallic properties show a continuum. This includes the trend from basic metal oxides through amphoteric to acidic non-metal oxides.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do substances such as CO₂, SO₂ and CaO simply dissolve in water without reacting?
items.correct: No. They react with water. CO₂ and SO₂ form acids (carbonic acid, sulfurous acid), which release H⁺ ions, so the pH falls; calcium oxide forms calcium hydroxide, CaO(s) + H₂O(l) → Ca(OH)₂(aq), so the pH rises.
items.misconception: A substance that dissolves in water, such as a gas or a metal oxide, does so physically, forming no new substance, so the solution stays neutral.
items.why: Dissolving is taught as a physical change, with salt and sugar as the everyday models, and fizzy drinks are described as 'water with carbon dioxide dissolved in it', so any substance disappearing into water seems to leave the water unchanged. Some substances react with the water they dissolve in: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ and SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃ give acids that lower the pH; CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ gives hydroxide ions that raise it. A change in indicator colour shows that a reaction has occurred.
items.specStatementText: Metallic and non-metallic properties show a continuum. This includes the trend from basic metal oxides through amphoteric to acidic non-metal oxides.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is acid rain the main cause of ocean acidification?
items.correct: No. Ocean acidification is caused mainly by the oceans absorbing carbon dioxide from the increased CO₂ in the atmosphere. Acid rain affects lakes, soils and buildings; its effect on the whole ocean is small.
items.misconception: Acid rain falling into the sea is what lowers the pH of seawater.
items.why: Both issues involve acids and fossil-fuel combustion, and environmental problems are commonly merged in students' minds, as reported in research on students' understanding of environmental issues. Keep the causes separate. Acid rain comes mainly from sulfur and nitrogen oxides. Ocean acidification comes from CO₂: CO₂(g) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂CO₃(aq), and carbonic acid releases H⁺ ions.
items.specStatementText: Metallic and non-metallic properties show a continuum. This includes the trend from basic metal oxides through amphoteric to acidic non-metal oxides.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does warmer water dissolve more carbon dioxide?
items.correct: No. The solubility of gases in water decreases as temperature increases, so warmer seawater dissolves less CO₂, not more.
items.misconception: Like most solids, gases dissolve better in warmer water.
items.why: Students' everyday experience is with solids such as sugar, which dissolve better in hot water, and they apply the same rule to gases. Gas solubility falls as temperature rises (a warm fizzy drink goes flat faster). The fall in seawater pH is caused by the rising concentration of CO₂ in the atmosphere, not by warming.
items.specStatementText: Metallic and non-metallic properties show a continuum. This includes the trend from basic metal oxides through amphoteric to acidic non-metal oxides.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is an oxidation state simply the actual charge on an ion, so that only ions have non-zero oxidation states?
items.correct: No. An oxidation state is the charge an atom would have if the compound were composed of ions. It is assigned to atoms in covalent molecules and in polyatomic ions too; for example nitrogen is +3 in NO₂⁻, even though the whole ion carries a 1− charge.
items.misconception: An oxidation state is the real charge on an ion, so it applies only to ions, and in a polyatomic ion the ion's charge is the oxidation state.
items.why: Oxidation states are first met for simple ions such as Na⁺ and Cl⁻, where the oxidation state does equal the ionic charge, so students conclude that the two are the same thing. Assign oxidation states by bookkeeping: the oxidation states of all atoms sum to zero in a compound and to the ion's charge in an ion. For NO₂⁻: x + 2(−2) = −1, so x = +3.
items.specStatementText: The oxidation state is a number assigned to an atom to show the number of electrons transferred in forming a bond. It is the charge that atom would have if the compound were composed of ions.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the nitrite ion NO₃⁻ and the nitrate ion NO₂⁻?
items.correct: No. Nitrate is NO₃⁻ (nitrogen +5) and nitrite is NO₂⁻ (nitrogen +3). Similarly sulfate is SO₄²⁻ (+6) and sulfite is SO₃²⁻ (+4). The '-ite' ion has the lower oxidation state and one fewer oxygen atom.
items.misconception: The '-ite' and '-ate' endings can be swapped, or '-ite' indicates the higher oxidation state.
items.why: The endings are arbitrary to a student and differ by a single letter, and both ions of each pair are often met in the same lesson. Learn the pairs with their oxidation states: nitrate NO₃⁻ (+5), nitrite NO₂⁻ (+3), sulfate SO₄²⁻ (+6), sulfite SO₃²⁻ (+4). '-ate' is the higher oxidation state; '-ite' the lower.
items.specStatementText: The oxidation state is a number assigned to an atom to show the number of electrons transferred in forming a bond. It is the charge that atom would have if the compound were composed of ions.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is oxygen −2 in a peroxide such as Na₂O₂ or H₂O₂?
items.correct: No. Oxygen is −1 in peroxides. The peroxide ion O₂²⁻ contains an O–O bond, so the 2− charge is shared between two oxygen atoms.
items.misconception: Oxygen in any compound containing oxygen and a metal is present as the oxide ion, O²⁻, so it is always −2.
items.why: Nearly every oxygen compound students meet is an oxide or oxyanion in which oxygen is −2, and the peroxide formula looks like an oxide with the numbers changed. Deduce, do not assume: in Na₂O₂, 2(+1) + 2x = 0, so x = −1. In H₂O₂, 2(+1) + 2x = 0, so x = −1. The O–O bond means the oxygen atoms share their electrons equally with each other.
items.specStatementText: The oxidation state is a number assigned to an atom to show the number of electrons transferred in forming a bond. It is the charge that atom would have if the compound were composed of ions.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does each element have one characteristic oxidation state set by its position in the periodic table?
items.correct: No. Many elements show several oxidation states (nitrogen from −3 to +5; sulfur −2, +4, +6; copper +1, +2), and even hydrogen and oxygen change in hydrides and peroxides. Every element is 0 when uncombined.
items.misconception: Each element has one fixed oxidation state, set by its group or its outer electrons (for example H +1, O −2, N +5, or Cu +1 from its single 4s electron), which it keeps in every compound.
items.why: Tables of 'usual' oxidation states are memorized as fixed values, and simple ionic compounds reinforce the idea that each element has one charge. Treat the usual values as a starting point, then check that the oxidation states sum to the overall charge. Where they do not, one of the usual values must change, as in hydrides, peroxides, and compounds of transition elements.
items.specStatementText: The oxidation state is a number assigned to an atom to show the number of electrons transferred in forming a bond. It is the charge that atom would have if the compound were composed of ions.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are all compounds of transition elements, and of d-block elements generally, coloured?
items.correct: No. Colour from electron promotion between split d orbitals needs a partly filled d sublevel, so compounds of Sc³⁺ (3d⁰) and Zn²⁺ (3d¹⁰) are white or colourless.
items.misconception: Every compound of a transition (d-block) element is coloured, whatever its oxidation state.
items.why: The most memorable transition element compounds (copper(II) sulfate, cobalt(II) chloride, iron(III) chloride) are strongly coloured, so colour becomes a defining label for the whole block. Colour in complexes arises when an electron is promoted between split d orbitals, which needs at least one electron and at least one vacancy in the d sublevel. Sc³⁺ (d⁰) and Zn²⁺ (d¹⁰) cannot absorb light in this way, so their compounds are colourless.
items.specStatementText: Transition elements have incomplete d-sublevels that give them characteristic properties.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a positive ion such as Fe²⁺ form by gaining electrons?
items.correct: No. A positive ion forms by losing electrons: Fe²⁺ has two electrons fewer than an Fe atom (24 instead of 26).
items.misconception: A positive charge means extra particles have been added, so a 2+ ion has gained two electrons.
items.why: The '+' sign suggests addition, and students unsure of the charge on an electron associate adding with positive. Electrons are negative. Removing negative charge leaves a positive ion: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻. Count electrons as Z minus the charge: 26 − 2 = 24.
items.specStatementText: The formation of variable oxidation states in transition elements can be explained by the fact that their successive ionization energies are close in value.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the colour of a transition element complex light emitted as electrons fall back between d orbitals?
items.correct: No. A complex is coloured because it absorbs some wavelengths of white light as electrons are promoted to higher split d orbitals; the colour seen is the light not absorbed.
items.misconception: Coloured compounds give out light of the colour we see, as in a flame test.
items.why: Flame tests and emission spectra are taught just before or alongside this topic, and both involve electron transitions and colour, so emission is carried over. Flame colours are emitted light from excited atoms at high temperature. A solution of a complex at room temperature is seen by the light it transmits: it absorbs the complementary colour and does not emit its own.
items.specStatementText: Transition element complexes are coloured due to the absorption of light when an electron is promoted between the orbitals in the split d-sublevels. The colour absorbed is complementary to the colour observed.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the colour of a transition element compound simply the colour of the metal ion itself, with no light absorbed?
items.correct: No. The colour depends on the absorption of visible light by electron promotion between split d orbitals, which depends on the metal ion, its oxidation state and the ligands. The same ion can have different colours with different ligands.
items.misconception: Colour is a fixed property of the metal ion, which is coloured in itself, like a dye.
items.why: Students learn lists of 'the colours of ions' (Cu²⁺ blue, Fe³⁺ yellow-brown) as facts, so colour seems to belong to the ion rather than to an interaction with light. Colour is the result of light being absorbed. Without light the solution has no colour, and changing the ligands changes the splitting and therefore the colour, as when [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ changes colour on adding ammonia or chloride ions.
items.specStatementText: Transition element complexes are coloured due to the absorption of light when an electron is promoted between the orbitals in the split d-sublevels. The colour absorbed is complementary to the colour observed.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is frequency found by dividing wavelength by the speed of light?
items.correct: No. From c = λf, f = c/λ. Dividing λ by c gives a quantity with units of seconds, not a frequency.
items.misconception: Frequency is the wavelength divided by the speed of light, f = λ/c.
items.why: Rearranging a three-term equation under time pressure, students divide the numbers in the order they appear, and they do not check the units of the answer. Rearrange c = λf by dividing both sides by λ: f = c/λ. Check the units: (m s⁻¹)/m = s⁻¹ = Hz. Dividing λ by c gives m/(m s⁻¹) = s, which is not a frequency.
items.specStatementText: Transition element complexes are coloured due to the absorption of light when an electron is promoted between the orbitals in the split d-sublevels. The colour absorbed is complementary to the colour observed.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is an ion about the same size as the atom it was formed from?
items.correct: No. A cation is much smaller than its atom and an anion is larger than its atom, because the ratio of nuclear charge to electrons changes and, for Na⁺ and Mg²⁺, a whole energy level is lost.
items.misconception: Forming an ion changes the charge but not the size, so ions keep the size order of their parent atoms.
items.why: Ion formation is taught as a change of charge, diagrams often draw an ion the same size as its atom, and students read ionic radii off the atomic-radius trend they have just learned. Compare nuclear charge with the number of electrons: losing the outer level makes Na⁺ and Mg²⁺ much smaller than their atoms; gaining electrons with the same nuclear charge makes O²⁻ and F⁻ larger than theirs.
items.specStatementText: Periodicity refers to trends in properties of elements across a period and down a group.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is hydrogen a halogen?
items.correct: No. The halogens are the group 17 elements, fluorine to astatine. Hydrogen, 1s¹, is not in group 17 and is not a halogen, although it forms H₂ molecules and, with reactive metals, the H⁻ ion.
items.misconception: Hydrogen belongs with the halogens because, like them, it is one electron short of a full shell, forms diatomic molecules and can form a 1− ion.
items.why: Some periodic tables place hydrogen above fluorine or in both groups 1 and 17, and the parallels H₂/X₂ and H⁻/X⁻ make the grouping look natural. Classify by group: the halogens are group 17, with ns² np⁵ configurations. Hydrogen has a single 1s electron and no p electrons, and is usually placed on its own or above group 1.
items.specStatementText: The period number shows the outer energy level that is occupied by electrons. Elements in a group have a common number of valence electrons.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does 'amphoteric' mean that an oxide is neutral and reacts with neither acids nor bases?
items.correct: No. An amphoteric oxide, such as aluminium oxide, reacts with both acids and bases. It sits between the basic and the acidic oxides in the continuum because it shows both kinds of behaviour, not neither.
items.misconception: An amphoteric oxide is neutral: lying between the basic and the acidic oxides, it reacts with neither acids nor bases.
items.why: Oxides are presented as a continuum from basic through amphoteric to acidic, and on the pH scale the point between acidic and alkaline is neutral, so 'in the middle' is read as 'neither'. Aluminium oxide's insolubility in water also makes it look unreactive. Read 'amphoteric' as 'both': Al₂O₃ reacts with acids such as hydrochloric acid and with bases such as sodium hydroxide. Oxides that react with neither, such as carbon monoxide, are called neutral oxides.
items.specStatementText: Metallic and non-metallic properties show a continuum. This includes the trend from basic metal oxides through amphoteric to acidic non-metal oxides.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does every oxide react with water to form an acid?
items.correct: No. Non-metal oxides such as CO₂ and SO₂ form acids, but group 1 and group 2 metal oxides form hydroxides, which give alkaline solutions: CaO(s) + H₂O(l) → Ca(OH)₂(aq).
items.misconception: All oxides react with water to form acids, as the oxides of carbon and sulfur do in acid rain.
items.why: Acid rain and ocean acidification make the reactions of non-metal oxides with water the most memorable oxide reactions in this topic, so 'oxide + water → acid' is generalized to every oxide, including those of metals. Decide from the element: group 1 and group 2 metal oxides are basic and form alkaline hydroxide solutions, non-metal oxides are acidic, and some oxides in between, such as Al₂O₃, are amphoteric.
items.specStatementText: Metallic and non-metallic properties show a continuum. This includes the trend from basic metal oxides through amphoteric to acidic non-metal oxides.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is every element of the d-block a transition element?
items.correct: No. Zinc, [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s², is in the d-block, but neither its atom nor its only ion, Zn²⁺ ([Ar] 3d¹⁰), has an incomplete d sublevel, so it is not a transition element.
items.misconception: Every metal in the d-block is a transition element, so 'transition element' and 'd-block element' mean the same thing.
items.why: Introductory courses and many periodic-table charts label the whole central block 'transition metals', including zinc, and the terms are used interchangeably until the incomplete-d-sublevel definition is met. Use the definition, not the position: a transition element has an incomplete d sublevel in its atom or in a common ion. In period 4 that is scandium to copper; zinc is a d-block element but not a transition element.
items.specStatementText: Transition elements have incomplete d-sublevels that give them characteristic properties.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a sulfur atom, [Ne] 3s² 3p⁴, have four valence electrons?
items.correct: No. It has six. The valence electrons are all the electrons in the outer energy level (n = 3): the two in 3s and the four in 3p.
items.misconception: The valence electrons are the electrons in the sublevel written last in the configuration, so [Ne] 3s² 3p⁴ has four and [Ne] 3s² 3p⁶ has six.
items.why: In the sublevel notation the last-written sublevel stands out as 'the outer one', and the words outer sublevel and outer energy level are easily merged. Students who first met valence electrons as a single number per group lose track of where the s electrons of the same level are counted. Add together every electron whose principal quantum number equals the period number. For period 3 elements that is 3s plus 3p: Mg 2, Al 3, Si 4, P 5, S 6, Cl 7, Ar 8. The group number of a p-block element is this total plus 10.
items.specStatementText: The period number shows the outer energy level that is occupied by electrons. Elements in a group have a common number of valence electrons.
